stem: A help desk platform adds a triage step that routes each incoming chat message to one of six queues before a human sees it. The step handles several million messages a day under a sub-second latency budget, and an eval on last month's traffic shows the smallest tier labels them as accurately as the larger ones. Which model choice fits this step?

options.text: The Haiku tier, since it is the fastest and cheapest and the eval shows it meets the bar
options.why: Correct. High-volume, narrow, latency-sensitive classification is the Haiku use case, and the eval confirms quality.

options.text: The Opus tier, so the triage step has the strongest reasoning as a safety margin
options.why: Pays for capability the eval shows is unneeded and adds latency and cost across millions of calls.

options.text: The Sonnet tier at max effort, balancing capability with extra reasoning per message
options.why: Max effort spends more tokens and time on a narrow task, working against the sub-second budget.

options.text: Whichever tier the rest of the platform uses, so that every step behaves consistently
options.why: Consistency is not a requirement here; each step's tier should fit its own volume and latency.

explanation: High volume, a narrow classification task and a sub-second budget describe the Haiku tier's use case, and the eval confirms quality holds. Defaulting to the most capable tier for a routing step is the classic overprovisioning mistake. Sonnet at max effort is tempting as a middle path, but max effort spends more tokens and time on exactly the dimension this step must minimise.
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: A team moves a code-review agent from an older Sonnet model to a newer generation by changing only the model string. The request still sends thinking type enabled with the budget_tokens value carried over from the old code, and every call now fails with a 400 pointing at the thinking configuration. What should they do?

options.text: Switch to adaptive thinking steered by effort, then evaluate two or three effort levels
options.why: Correct. Newer generations replace manual budgets with adaptive thinking and effort, and no fixed budget-to-effort mapping exists.

options.text: Retry the failed calls with exponential backoff until the new model accepts the request
options.why: A 400 is a validation error about request shape; an identical retry fails identically.

options.text: Lower budget_tokens to the 1,024 minimum so the manual thinking request passes validation
options.why: The newer model rejects manual thinking budgets altogether, so the value is not what fails.

options.text: Revert permanently to the older model ID so the existing thinking configuration keeps working
options.why: Every model ID has its own retirement schedule; reverting postpones a migration that still has to happen.

explanation: Newer generations replace manual thinking budgets with adaptive thinking controlled by effort, so a carried-over budget_tokens request is a request-shape error, not a transient fault. There is no fixed mapping from a budget to an effort level, so the migration should evaluate a few levels against the existing suite. Shrinking the budget is tempting because the error names the thinking block, but manual mode itself is what the newer model rejects.
cue: still sends thinking type enabled with the budget_tokens value carried over

postGuide.note: budget_tokens returning a 400 applies to the Claude 4.7-and-later generations. At guide time, manual budgets were deprecated on the 4.6 models but still accepted. Engineering knowledge, low exam confidence.

stem: An invoice extractor sets temperature to 0 and relies on a prompt instruction to get JSON back. After the model ID is moved to a newer release, every request returns a 400 naming the temperature parameter, and the accounts system downstream must receive JSON that matches a fixed schema. What should the team do?

options.text: Remove temperature and enforce the schema with structured outputs, then re-run the extraction evals
options.why: Correct. The sampling setting has to go, and a must-match schema needs an enforced control rather than an instruction.

options.text: Set temperature to 0.01 so the value is accepted while keeping near-deterministic output
options.why: The newer release rejects any non-default sampling value, so 0.01 fails the same way.

options.text: Remove temperature and strengthen the prompt instruction to always return valid JSON
options.why: Clears the 400 but leaves schema compliance as a request; a must-match requirement needs enforcement.

options.text: Revert to the older model ID and keep temperature 0 as the consistency guarantee
options.why: Temperature 0 never guaranteed consistent output, and the older ID will eventually retire.

explanation: The newer release rejects non-default sampling parameters, so temperature has to go, and the downstream must-match requirement calls for an enforced control rather than an instruction. Structured outputs constrain the response to the JSON schema. Removing temperature and tightening the prompt is tempting because it clears the 400, but a prompt is a request and only the schema is a guarantee.
cue: must receive JSON that matches a fixed schema

postGuide.note: Non-default temperature, top_p and top_k returning a 400 (Claude Opus 4.7 and later, Sonnet 5 and later) landed after the July 2026 guide. Engineering knowledge, not exam content.

author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: A contract-comparison workflow runs on a Sonnet model at high effort, and its release evals were all tuned against that configuration. To cut latency, an engineer proposes moving it to the Haiku tier at low effort, expecting similar quality. What is the main problem with the proposal?

options.text: The Haiku tier has no effort parameter at all, and a tier swap voids evals tuned on Sonnet
options.why: Correct. Haiku is differently shaped, not just cheaper, and any model change invalidates evaluated behaviour.

options.text: The Haiku tier requires adaptive thinking to be enabled before any effort level takes effect
options.why: Backwards: the Haiku model rejects adaptive thinking and supports thinking only through manual budgets.

options.text: Low effort disables thinking on every tier, so quality would drop whichever model is used
options.why: Effort is a behavioural signal; at low effort Claude still thinks on sufficiently difficult problems.

options.text: The Haiku tier has a lower output ceiling, so comparison reports would be cut off at length
options.why: Its maximum output is lower than Sonnet's but ample for reports like these; it is not the main problem.

explanation: Haiku is differently shaped, not just cheaper: it takes thinking only through manual budgets and has no effort parameter, so 'Haiku at low effort' is not a valid request. Even setting that aside, a tier swap changes the model the evals measured. The better first move for latency is lowering effort on the current Sonnet model and re-running the suite.
cue: moving it to the Haiku tier at low effort
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: A team is prototyping an autonomous agent that will refactor a large legacy codebase over several hours of tool use. Nobody yet knows whether any model can complete the task, and per-task cost is secondary to finding out. Which starting point fits?

options.text: Start on the Opus tier, optimise prompts, then lower effort or downgrade while evals hold
options.why: Correct. Capability-first fits complex, high-autonomy work where feasibility is unproven and accuracy outweighs cost.

options.text: Start on the Haiku tier and move up a tier each time the agent fails a refactoring run
options.why: Efficiency-first suits simple, cost-sensitive work; failures here cannot separate a capability gap from a prompt problem.

options.text: Start on the Sonnet tier at low effort, raising effort only after the first runs succeed
options.why: Low effort handicaps a feasibility test, so early failures could wrongly mark the task as infeasible.

options.text: Run all three tiers in production from day one and keep whichever finishes the most tasks
options.why: Feasibility is a development question; shipping unevaluated agents to production adds risk and cost.

explanation: When feasibility is the open question and accuracy outweighs cost, Anthropic describes starting capability-first: use the strongest model, get it working, then lower effort or downgrade while evals hold. Starting on the smallest tier is the efficiency-first path, which fits cost-sensitive, straightforward work. Its failures here would not tell the team whether the task or the model was the limit.
cue: Nobody yet knows whether any model can complete the task
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: A research assistant uses an Opus-tier orchestrator that plans each query and synthesises the findings, and it fans out to dozens of subagents that each extract facts from one source. The subagent tasks are narrow and well specified, and their combined tokens make up most of the bill. Which change best fits the tradeoff?

options.text: Run the subagents on the Haiku tier and keep the orchestrator on Opus, confirming with evals
options.why: Correct. Narrow, high-volume sub-agent work is a Haiku use case, while planning and synthesis justify Opus.

options.text: Move the orchestrator to the Haiku tier as well, so the whole system runs on the cheapest model
options.why: Planning and synthesis are where capability matters most; the orchestrator is not the dominant cost.

options.text: Raise the subagents' effort to max so each extraction finishes in a single tool call
options.why: Max effort raises token spend on narrow tasks, moving the dominant cost in the wrong direction.

options.text: Enable fast mode on the subagents so their share of the bill is processed more quickly
options.why: Fast mode buys output speed at premium per-token prices; it raises cost instead of lowering it.

explanation: Narrow, well-specified, high-volume work is the Haiku tier's use case, including sub-agent tasks, while planning and synthesis justify the stronger orchestrator. Splitting tiers by role cuts the dominant cost without touching the part that needs deep reasoning, and evals confirm the subagents still extract correctly. Moving the orchestrator down as well is tempting for symmetry, but it puts the hardest work on the least capable model.
cue: The subagent tasks are narrow and well specified
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: Product wants a support bot's reasoning depth to scale with question difficulty. The bot runs on the Haiku tier with manual thinking at a fixed budget, so an engineer replaces that block with thinking type adaptive and ships the change. What is the most likely result, and the right fix?

options.text: Requests fail with a 400; move the route to a tier that supports adaptive thinking and re-run evals
options.why: Correct. The Haiku model rejects adaptive thinking, so scaling reasoning means a model change gated by evals.

options.text: Requests succeed, but the tier ignores the adaptive setting and keeps thinking at the old budget
options.why: Unsupported request shapes fail validation with a 400; they are not silently downgraded.

options.text: Requests fail until effort is also set, since adaptive thinking on this tier needs an effort level
options.why: The Haiku model has no effort parameter, so adding one would introduce a second invalid field.

options.text: Requests succeed and thinking now scales per request, since every current tier supports adaptive mode
options.why: Adaptive thinking is not universal: the Haiku model supports only manual extended thinking.

explanation: Adaptive thinking is not supported on every tier: the Haiku model takes thinking only through manual budget_tokens and returns a 400 for adaptive. Scaling reasoning with difficulty therefore means moving the route to a tier that supports adaptive thinking, which is a model change that needs evals. The silently-ignored option is tempting, but unsupported request shapes fail validation rather than degrading quietly.
cue: The bot runs on the Haiku tier with manual thinking
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: A platform team is writing a routing library that attaches thinking settings to requests for Haiku, Sonnet and Opus routes. The library must never send a request shape that a tier rejects. Which two rules should it encode? Select two.

options.text: Omit the effort parameter on Haiku routes, because that tier does not support it
options.why: Correct. The models overview lists effort as not supported on the Haiku model.

options.text: On Haiku routes, request thinking with type enabled and a budget_tokens value of at least 1,024
options.why: Correct. Manual extended thinking is the Haiku model's only thinking mode, with a 1,024-token minimum budget.

options.text: Send thinking type adaptive on every route, because all current tiers accept it
options.why: The Haiku model returns a 400 for adaptive thinking, so this shape fails on one tier.

options.text: Map effort by tier, sending low for Haiku, medium for Sonnet and high for Opus
options.why: Looks like sensible tuning, but sending any effort value to Haiku is a shape that tier does not support.

options.text: Use budget_tokens on every route, so one request shape works for all three tiers
options.why: Manual budgets are deprecated on the 4.6 models and rejected on later ones, so one shared shape is not valid.

explanation: Thinking controls are not uniform across tiers: the Haiku model has no effort parameter and supports thinking only through manual budgets (minimum 1,024, below max_tokens), while current Sonnet and Opus models use adaptive thinking and effort. A single shared shape cannot be valid everywhere. Mapping effort by tier is tempting because it looks like sensible tuning, but sending effort to Haiku is exactly the unsupported shape.
cue: must never send a request shape that a tier rejects
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: An insurer extracts fields from claim emails, and each wrong extraction costs $0.60 of reviewer time to correct. On the Haiku tier a request costs $0.004 and 10% of outputs are wrong, while on the Sonnet tier a request costs $0.012 and 2% are wrong; errors are found only when a reviewer later spots them, not by any automated check. Which choice minimises cost per completed task?

options.text: The Sonnet tier, at about $0.024 per completed task against about $0.064 on Haiku
options.why: Correct. $0.012 + 2% of $0.60 is $0.024, while $0.004 + 10% of $0.60 is $0.064 per completed task.

options.text: The Haiku tier, since its requests cost a third of Sonnet's and volume dominates spend
options.why: Ignores the correction cost: ten times more errors at $0.60 each outweighs the cheaper request.

options.text: Haiku first with escalation of failed outputs to Sonnet, at roughly $0.005 per task
options.why: A cascade needs machine-detectable failures to escalate, and here no automated check can flag them.

options.text: The Opus tier, since its lower error rate will outweigh any difference in request price
options.why: No error rate is given for Opus, so the claim is unsupported at a higher price per request.

explanation: Cost per completed task includes handling failures: Haiku is $0.004 + 10% x $0.60 = $0.064 and Sonnet is $0.012 + 2% x $0.60 = $0.024. The cascade looks cheapest, but it works only when failures are machine-detectable, and here nothing flags a bad extraction until a person finds it. The lowest price per request is the trap the numbers are built to expose.
cue: errors are found only when a reviewer later spots them
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: A document Q&A route on a Sonnet model passes its release evals, but finance needs its per-request cost cut this quarter. The release process treats any change of model ID as a new model that needs six weeks of re-certification. What should the team try first?

options.text: Lower effort on the same model and re-run all the existing evals at the new level
options.why: Correct. Effort trades thoroughness for tokens within one model, so the model ID and its certification stay put.

options.text: Move the route to the Haiku tier, which costs less per token for the same prompts
options.why: A tier change is a model ID change, which triggers the six-week re-certification.

options.text: Enable fast mode on the route so each request finishes and bills more quickly
options.why: Fast mode charges premium per-token prices; it raises cost rather than cutting it.

options.text: Cut max_tokens until the average bill per request meets the finance target
options.why: A lower cap truncates answers instead of making them efficient, which will fail the evals.

explanation: Effort trades thoroughness against token spend within one model, and Anthropic notes it is often a better lever than switching models. Keeping the model ID avoids the six-week re-certification, and re-running the existing suite at the lower level confirms quality holds. Moving to Haiku is the tempting cost answer, but it is exactly the model change the release process treats as new.
cue: treats any change of model ID as a new model
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: A ticket classifier forces JSON output by ending every request with an assistant turn that contains only an opening brace. After the model ID is moved to a newer generation, every call fails with a 400 saying the conversation must end with a user message. Which replacement keeps the output machine-parseable?

options.text: Drop the assistant turn and constrain the reply with structured outputs and a JSON schema
options.why: Correct. Structured outputs are the documented replacement for format-forcing prefill and enforce the shape.

options.text: Keep the assistant turn but add a stop sequence on the closing brace to end output cleanly
options.why: The final assistant turn is still a prefill, so the 400 remains, and a stop sequence does not enforce JSON.

options.text: Retry the failed calls with exponential backoff, since the new model is still rolling out
options.why: A 400 is a validation error about request shape; it is not transient and retries fail identically.

options.text: Move the brace into the system prompt as an instruction to begin every reply with it
options.why: Clears the 400 but turns an enforced format into a request the model may not follow.

explanation: From the 4.6 generation, a prefilled final assistant turn returns a 400, so the conversation has to end with a user message. Anthropic's migration advice for format-forcing prefill is structured outputs, which constrain the reply to a schema. Turning the prefill into an instruction is tempting because it clears the error, but it downgrades an enforced format to a request.
cue: ending every request with an assistant turn
author: agent:q-llm-models

stem: A team plans to move a contract-review service from one model release to the next. The head of legal requires that review accuracy must not regress, and operations wants a fast rollback path if it does. Which two steps belong in the plan? Select two.

options.text: Re-run the review eval suite on the new model at two or three effort levels before promoting
options.why: Correct. Must-not-regress makes evals the gate, and effort levels do not map one to one across releases.

options.text: Pin both model IDs in configuration and canary the new one behind a flag with rollback
options.why: Correct. Pinned IDs in config plus a flagged canary give operations an immediate rollback path.

options.text: Point the service at a dateless alias so future releases are picked up without a deploy
options.why: Older-style aliases move to newer snapshots, letting a model change reach production without the eval gate.

options.text: Reuse the existing token budgets, since tokenization does not change between releases
options.why: Newer generations use a tokenizer that produces about 30% more tokens, so budgets must be recounted.

options.text: Retry any 400 errors during rollout with backoff, since new releases warm up gradually
options.why: A 400 signals a rejected request shape on the new model, which retries cannot fix.

explanation: 'Must not regress' makes the eval suite the gate, and an effort sweep is needed because levels do not map one to one across releases. Pinning IDs in configuration and canarying behind a flag gives the rollback path. The alias option is tempting because it removes deploys, but it lets a model change reach production without passing the gate legal required.
author: agent:q-llm-models
